q-164468.problem:
$$
f(y,z)=⟨\text{_____},\,y,\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(y,z)$ above parametrizes the hyperbolic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $2x=3{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}.$ What is the first component of $f?$
q-164468.worked_solution:
Solving our equation for $x,$ we obtain

$$
2x=3{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2},\,y,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.$

Question 1
?

f(y,z)=⟨_____,y,z⟩

The vector-valued function f(y,z) above parametrizes the hyperbolic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as 2x=3y2−4z2. What is the first component of f?

a
34y2−z2
b
32y2−2z2
c
y2−2z2
d
32y2−4z2
e
3y2−2z2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Solving our equation for x, we obtain

2x=3y2−4z2⟹x=32y2−2z2.

Now, for any point (x,y,z) on our surface, we obtain the following:

f(y,z)=⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨32y2−2z2,y,z⟩

where y∈(−∞,∞) and z∈(−∞,∞).

Therefore, the first component of f is 32y2−2z2.

$$
f(x,z)=⟨x,\,\text{_____},\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(x,z)$ above parametrizes the hyperbolic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $2y=8{z}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$ What is the second component of $f?$
q-104328.worked_solution:
Solving our equation for $y,$ we obtain

$$
2y=8{z}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,y=4{z}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨x,\,4{z}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $x\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $4{z}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.$

q-164463.problem:
$$
f(x,y)=⟨x,\,y,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(x,y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\frac{z}{2}=3{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}.$ What is the third component of $f?$
q-164463.worked_solution:
Solving our equation for $z,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{z}{2}=3{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\,⟹\,z=6{x}^{2}+8{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨x,\,y,\,6{x}^{2}+8{y}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

f(x,y)=⟨x,y,_____⟩

The vector-valued function f(x,y) above parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as z2=3x2+4y2. What is the third component of f?

b

c
 6x2+8y2
d
32x2+2y2
e
3x2+14y2
Submit

Solving our equation for z, we obtain

z2=3x2+4y2⟹z=6x2+8y2.

Now, for any point (x,y,z) on our surface, we obtain the following:

f(x,y)=⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨x,y,6x2+8y2⟩

Therefore, the third component of f is 6x2+8y2.

$$
5x=10{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\,⟹\,x=2{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}{z}^{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨2{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}{z}^{2},\,y,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $2{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}{z}^{2}.$

q-164540.name: Question 6
q-164540.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta ),$ given by

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨{r}^{2},\,\text{_____},\,4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as

$$
x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}.
$$

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=Z,\,y=3X,\,z=4Y
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$
q-164540.worked_solution:
First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=Z,\,y=3X,\,z=4Y
$$

into our equation, we get

$$
Z={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & ={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2} \\ Z & =(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\ Z & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\ Z & ={r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r,\theta ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨Z,3X,4Y⟩ \\  & =⟨Z,\,3r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨{r}^{2},\,3r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $r\in [0,\infty )$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $3r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

q-164537.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta ),$ given by

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{r}^{2},\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}.
$$

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=2Y,\,y=Z,\,z=4X
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the third component of $f.$
q-164537.worked_solution:
First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=2Y,\,y=Z,\,z=4X
$$

 

into our equation, we get

$$
Z={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & ={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2} \\ Z & =(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\ Z & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\ Z & ={r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r,\theta ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨2Y,Z,4X⟩ \\  & =⟨2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z,\,4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{r}^{2},\,4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $r\in [0,\infty )$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as z=x225+y24. By first considering the transformations x=5X,y=2Y,z=Z

q-164529.name: Question 10
q-164529.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta ),$ given by

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____},\,{r}^{2}⟩
$$

parametrizes the elliptic paraboloid defined in Cartesian coordinates as 

$$
z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}.
$$

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=4X,\,y=\sqrt{3}Y,\,z=Z
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$
q-164529.worked_solution:
First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=4X,\,y=\sqrt{3}Y,\,z=Z
$$

into our equation, we get

$$
Z={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & ={X}^{2}+{Y}^{2} \\ Z & =(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\ Z & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\ Z & ={r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r,\theta ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4X,\sqrt{3}Y,Z⟩ \\  & =⟨4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{3}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z⟩ \\  & =⟨4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{3}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{r}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $r\in [0,\infty )$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $\sqrt{3}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

q-164588.name: Question 11
q-164588.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by 

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨\text{_____},5\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,7\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

parametrizes the hyperboloid of one sheet defined in Cartesian coordinates as 

$$
-{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{49}=1.
$$

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=Z,\,y=5Y,\,z=7X
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the first component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${r}^{2}-{Z}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨r,Z⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$
q-164588.worked_solution:
First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=Z,\,y=5Y,\,z=7X
$$

into our equation, we get

$$
{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2}=1.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=Z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{Z}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${r}^{2}-{Z}^{2}=1$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $Z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $X$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨r,Z⟩=⟨\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨Z,5Y,7X⟩ \\  & =⟨Z,\,5r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,7r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ,\,5(\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,7(\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ,\,5\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,7\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ.$

q-164584.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\,\text{_____},\,5\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as 

$$
-\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}+{y}^{2}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{25}=-1.
$$

 

By first considering the transformations

$$
x=6Z,\,y=Y,\,z=5X
$$

and writing the resulting system in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${Z}^{2}-{r}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨Z,r⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$

First, substituting the transformations

$$
x=6Z,\,y=Y,\,z=5X
$$

into our equation, we get

$$
{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2}=-1.
$$

If $(r,\theta ,Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
X=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,Y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,Z=Z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}-{Z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {Z}^{2}-{r}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${Z}^{2}-{r}^{2}=1$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $Z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $X$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨Z,r⟩=⟨\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨6Z,Y,5X⟩ \\  & =⟨6Z,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,5\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

q-164578.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by 

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨\text{_____},\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=-1.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the first component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${z}^{2}-{r}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨z,r⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$
q-164578.worked_solution:
If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {r}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-1 \\ {z}^{2}-{r}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${z}^{2}-{r}^{2}=1$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $x$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨z,r⟩=⟨\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩ \\  & =⟨(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by 

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____},\,6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩
$$

parametrizes one sheet of the hyperboloid of two sheets defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=-36.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$
q-164579.worked_solution:
If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-36 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-36 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{z}^{2} & =-36 \\ {r}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =-36 \\ {z}^{2}-{r}^{2} & =36\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${z}^{2}-{r}^{2}=36$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $x$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨z,r⟩=⟨6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩ \\  & =⟨(6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,6\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $6\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
